extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and natural philosophers interested in observational astronomy, geognosy, and the methodology of physical science (19th-century scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Methodological principles and standards for observational astronomy and geognosy: how to infer distances, masses, structures, and history of celestial and terrestrial bodies from measurements, instrument limits, and comparative reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for firm observational methods over vague conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Human inquiry need no longer pursue this subject in the domain of vague conjecture, or amid the undefined analogies of the ideal world; for even here the progress made in the method of astronomical observations and calculations has enabled astronomy to take up its position on a firm basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise astronomical observations and calculations as the basis for conclusions about celestial phenomena (e.g., motion of double stars, retarded or accelerated motion in elliptic orbits), rather than relying on vague analogies or conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive orbital elements from altered distances and position angles
rubrics_metrics.description: By a skillful combination of the altered distances and angles of position, the elements of these orbits may be found, conclusions drawn regarding the absolute distance of the double stars from the Earth, and comparisons made between their mass and that of the Sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine changes in separations and position angles over time to compute orbital elements, absolute distances, and relative masses of binary systems; careful repeated positional measurement is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parallax measurements to determine stellar distances and infer masses
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance of the star 61 Cygni, made known by Bessel, has led approximately to a knowledge of the quantity of matter contained in this body as a double star...it has been conjectured with much probability...that the mass of this double star can not be very considerably larger or smaller than half of the mass of the Sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on measured parallaxes to estimate distances, and use those distances together with orbital data to infer masses; acknowledge limitations when observed arc is small or data incomplete (Bradley's observations did not traverse a sufficient portion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat apparent stellar diameters as extremely uncertain optical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparison of the volume of the Sun with that of the fixed stars of the first magnitude is dependent upon the apparent diameter of the latter bodies -- an extremely undertain optical element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using apparent angular diameters to infer true diameters/volumes; note optical and instrumental uncertainties (example: Herschel's assumption about Arcturus' apparent diameter leading to large inferred true diameter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative statistics of observed samples to infer population properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The analogies deduced from the relatively larger mass of those planets in our solar system that are attended by satellites, and from the fact that Struve has discovered six times more double stars among the brighter than among the telescopic fixed stars, have led other astronomers to conjecture that the average mass of the larger number of the binary stars exceeds the mass of the Sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare frequencies and properties across observationally-defined samples (e.g., bright vs telescopic stars) to hypothesize about population-level properties, but account for selection effects and observational biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for proper motion and long-term dynamics in interpreting celestial appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: The aspect of the starry heavens, the relative position of stars and nebullae, the distribution of their luminous masses... depend in the course of ages conjointly upon the proper motion of the stars and nebulae, the translation of our solar system in space, the appearance of new stars, and the disappearance or sudden diminution in the intensity of the light of others, and lastly and specially, on the changes which the Earth's axis experiences from the attraction of the Sun and Moon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting star distributions and the 'aspect' of the heavens, include effects of stellar proper motion, solar system translation, transient events (new or vanishing stars), and precession/nutation of Earth's axis; predictions (e.g., future pole stars) should be based on these dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for finite speed of light when interpreting observations (penetrating time as well as space)
rubrics_metrics.description: With our large and powerful telescopic instruments we penetrate alike through the boundaries of time and space: we measure the former through the latter...a ray of light traverses over a space of 592 millions of miles [in an hour]...the light of remote heavenly bodies presents us with the most ancient perceptible evidence of the existence of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that observations show past states of distant objects; incorporate light-travel time into chronological interpretation of celestial phenomena (e.g., novae observed are events from centuries ago at large distances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider telescope resolving power and instrument limits when classifying nebulae vs stars
rubrics_metrics.description: In whatever part the vault of heaven has been pierced by powerful and far-penetrating telescopic instruments, stars or luminous nebulae are every where discoverable, the former, in some cases, not exceeding the twentieth or twenty-fourth degree of telescopic magnitude. A portion of the nebulous vapor would probably be found resolvable into stars by more powerful optical instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to revise classifications of 'nebulae' or 'nebulous stars' as instrument resolution improves; classification depends on current telescope power and may change with better optics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for photometric and perceptual effects on apparent brightness and resolvability
rubrics_metrics.description: As the retina retains a less vivid impression of separate than of infinitely near luminous points, less strongly marked photometric relations are excited in the latter case, as Arago has recently shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging aggregated light vs resolved points, consider physiological perception and photometric effects (human retina response) in interpreting the apparent luminosity and degree of resolution of celestial objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret starless 'openings' as evidence of large-scale inhomogeneity and agglomeration
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption of [a uniform distribution of stars] is... at variance with observation, which shows us large starless regions of space, 'openings' in the heavens, as William Herschel terms them...Herschel ascribes these openings or starless regions to the attractive and agglomerative forces of the marginal groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed large starless regions and surrounding unresolvable nebulae to infer inhomogeneous distributions, agglomeration processes, and to identify directions where telescopes may look deeper into space (tubes to remotest depths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and distinguish 'absolute depth' vs 'relative depth' in subsurface reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: In speaking of the greatest depths within the Earth reached by human labor, we must recollect that there is a difference between the 'absolute depth' (that is to say, the depth below the Earth's surface at that point) and the 'relative depth' (or that beneath the level of the sea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting depths of borings/mines/wells, explicitly state whether depths are absolute (below local surface) or relative (below sea level), since temperature and other inferences depend on the reference datum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer deep subterranean structures from surface strata dips and bore data
rubrics_metrics.description: We are able to give in numbers the depth of the shaft where the strata of coal, after penetrating a certain way, rise again at a distance that admits of being accurately defined by measurements. These dips show that the carboniferous strata... must lie... below the present level of the sea, and that the calcareous and the curved strata of the Devonian basin penetrate twice that depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measured dips, reappearance distances, basin-shaped curved strata, and borehole results together to infer depths and geometry of subsurface basins beyond direct human reach; such testimony has great geognostic interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct contact (surface access) for detailed physical and chemical characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Their physical character is, however, hidden in obscurity, for it is only in our own globe that we can be brought in immediate contact with all the elements of organic and inorganic creation...The physical description of celestial bodies...is limited... No manifestation of vital activity is there presented to our senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give greater weight to observations and measurements obtainable by direct contact (mining, sampling, laboratory analysis) when characterizing material properties, chemistry, and complex phenomena; remote observation (astronomy) provides more limited characterization (volume, mass, motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy and inductive combination of phenomena to advance geognosy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is by a combination of actual phenomena, by an ideal enlargement of relations in space, and of the amount of active forces, that we are able to advance into the long sought and indefinitely anticipated domain of geognosy, which has only within the last half century been based on the solid foundation of scientific deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine direct observations, analogical reasoning, and idealized extrapolations of spatial relations and forces to construct geognostic theories; base such inductive generalizations on accumulated empirical evidence.
